newsitem.title: USA: Consumers boost credit-buying briskly in April.
newsitem.headline: Consumers boost credit-buying briskly in April.

text.p: Consumers continued to boost their credit-buying at a brisk rate in April, the Federal Reserve said Friday, largely on a surge in auto loans that may soon level off.
Total consumer instalment credit, or loans that require monthly payments, rose by $7.6 billion, or a 7.6 percent annual rate in April.

That was more than double a revised $3.1 billion increase in March when instalment loans grew at a 3 percent pace. Previously, the Fed said March credit had risen by $2 billion but it pushed that estimate up.

A surprising bulge in auto loans during April, which soared $4 billion at a 12.7 percent annual rate for the strongest monthly rise since July last year, was the primary reason for the overall monthly increase. Auto credit had contracted by $900 million at a 2.7 percent rate in March.
Robert Dederick, economic consultant to Northern Trust Co. in Chicago, said stronger auto loans seemed oddly inconsistent with automakers' reports of weaker spring sales of new cars and trucks.
Some of it may reflect accounting delays in reflecting loans for earlier sales on banks' and other lenders' books, he added, so that auto credit may soon slow down.

"The basic message seems to be that notwithstanding the numbers pickup in April, moderation is the theme," Dederick said. He noted that after shooting up by $10.3 billion in January, consumer credit grew at a lower average of $5.8 billion a month in the three months from February through April.

"What this suggests is that consumers are not acting overly aggressively and we're seeing no evidence of distress borrowing," Dederick said. "Consumers seem to be managing credit, in the aggregate, more conservatively than they were earlier."
During April, revolving or credit-card credit rose by $1.8 billion at a 4.3 percent annual rate. Credit-card debts had risen $1.5 billion at a 3.9 percent rate in March.

Other credit, which includes bank loans for mobile homes, education and other things but not mortgages, rose by $2 billion at a 6.6 percent annual rate in April. In March, this category of credit was up $2.4 billion at an 8 percent annual rate.
